The idea is that verification accepts several keys while signing uses only one. Each token carries a key ID (`kid`) in its header, so the verifier can tell which key to check it against.

1. **Add `kid` support, if you don't have it.** Make verifiers look up the key by the token's `kid`. Tokens issued before that change have no `kid`, so check them against the current (old) key.
2. **Deploy the new key to every verifier first, and keep signing with the old one.** Each verifier then holds `{old, new}`. With asymmetric keys (RS256 or ES256), add the new public key to your JWKS endpoint, and wait for verifiers' JWKS caches to expire before going on.
3. **Switch the signer to the new key.** Do this only after every verifier has it. If you switch first, verifiers that haven't updated will reject the new tokens and log those users out.
4. **Wait out the longest token lifetime, then remove the old key.** "Longest" includes refresh tokens if they are JWTs signed with this same key. A 30-day refresh token means the old key stays in the verify set for 30 days. You can shorten that by re-issuing refresh tokens with the new key whenever they are used.

The ordering is the whole trick: verifiers before the signer, and old-key removal only after the last old token has expired.

**If you are rotating because the key leaked, this approach is wrong.** Keeping the old key valid also keeps valid any tokens an attacker forged with it. Remove the old key immediately and accept that sessions will end. The exception is opaque refresh tokens stored in your database: those don't depend on the signing key, so clients can use them to get new access tokens signed with the new key, and users stay logged in.

Callers get tokens from `currentToken()`, which calls `refresh()` when the token is close to expiry. A module-level promise makes concurrent refreshes share one network call. Nothing in `auth.js` reacts to a 401 from an ordinary API request; the only 401 it handles comes from the token endpoint.

### Normal path (`auth.js:6-10`)

Each request calls `currentToken(store)`. If the stored access token has more than 30 seconds left (`SKEW_MS`), it is returned without a network call. Otherwise it calls `refresh(store)`, and it does the same when there is no access token at all. Attaching the token to requests and reading their responses happen outside this file, despite the comment on line 1.

### Refresh (`auth.js:12-38`)

1. If a refresh is already running, `refresh()` returns that refresh's promise (line 13).
2. It reads the refresh token. If there isn't one, it throws `no refresh token; re-auth required` without making a request.
3. It POSTs `grant_type: refresh_token` to `/oauth/token` as a JSON body and stores the promise in `inFlight`.
4. On success, it stores the new access token. `expiresAt` is `expires_in` added to the local clock, so a server clock that disagrees with yours doesn't matter. If the response includes a new refresh token (rotation), it replaces the old one; otherwise the old one stays. The promise resolves with the access token.
5. Whatever the outcome, `.finally` sets `inFlight` back to `null`. That reset is part of the chain callers are awaiting, so `inFlight` is already `null` when any caller resumes.

### On a 401

A 401 from `/oauth/token` triggers `store.clear()`. That wipes the access token, the refresh token and anything else in the store, and the promise rejects with `refresh rejected; re-auth required`. Every later call then fails at step 2 until the user signs in again.

Any other error status (line 25) rejects with `refresh failed: <status>` and leaves the store alone. The next request will try again with the same refresh token, with no backoff.

Two things change how this behaves in practice:

- **API 401s are ignored.** Nothing retries after a 401 from your API. If the server revokes an access token that still looks valid locally, callers keep sending it until it gets within 30 seconds of expiry, unless the caller calls the exported `refresh()` itself.

### Two requests refreshing at once

Request A finds the token stale and calls `refresh()`. `inFlight` is `null`, so A starts the fetch and sets `inFlight`. Request B arrives before the response comes back, also sees the stale token, and calls `refresh()`. Line 13 hands B the same promise A has. There is one network call, and both requests get the same token or the same error. Line 13 checks `inFlight` and line 16 sets it with no `await` in between, so a second fetch can't sneak in within one JavaScript runtime.

The module has two functions. `currentToken` decides whether a refresh is needed, and `refresh` performs it and makes sure only one runs at a time.

## Normal flow

1. **`currentToken(store)`** (`auth.js:6`) reads `store.get('access')`. If the token exists and expires more than `SKEW_MS` (30 seconds) from now, it returns `t.value` straight away. If the token is missing, expired, or within 30 seconds of expiring, it calls `refresh(store)`.
2. **`refresh(store)`** (`auth.js:12`) first checks `inFlight`. If a refresh is already running, it returns that same promise (covered below).
3. Otherwise it reads `store.get('refresh')`. If there is no refresh token, it throws `'no refresh token; re-auth required'`. Since `refresh` is `async`, this reaches the caller as a rejected promise.
4. It POSTs `{ grant_type: 'refresh_token', refresh_token: rt.value }` to `/oauth/token` and saves the resulting promise chain in `inFlight`.
5. On a successful response, it stores the new access token with `expiresAt = Date.now() + expires_in * 1000`. The clock starts when the response arrives, not when the request was sent. If the server sent a new `refresh_token` (rotation), that is stored too; if not, the old one is kept. It then resolves with the new access token.
6. The `.finally` sets `inFlight = null` whether the refresh succeeded or failed.

## What happens on a 401

The only 401 this file handles is a 401 from **`/oauth/token` itself**, meaning the refresh token was rejected. When that happens, `store.clear()` deletes both tokens and the promise rejects with `'refresh rejected; re-auth required'`. Any later call then fails at step 3 with `'no refresh token; re-auth required'`.

Other failures are handled differently:
- **Non-401 errors** (such as a 500) reject with `'refresh failed: ' + res.status`. The store is not touched, so the next call simply tries again, with no backoff.
- **Network errors** reject with fetch's own `TypeError`, unwrapped, and the store is also left alone.

A 401 from an actual **API request** is not handled anywhere in this file. Nothing here retries the request or forces a refresh. If the server revokes an access token before its `expiresAt`, `currentToken` keeps returning it until the local expiry check fails. A caller that wants to refresh on an API 401 would have to call the exported `refresh` itself. Despite the comment at line 1, this module never touches outbound requests; it only hands out tokens. This directory contains only `auth.js`, so I couldn't check whether any caller does this.

## Two requests refreshing at once

Say requests A and B both call `currentToken` and both find the token expired:

- A enters `refresh`, sees that `inFlight` is null, reads the refresh token, starts the fetch, and assigns `inFlight`. All of this runs synchronously, with no `await` before the assignment, so B cannot run in the middle of it.
- B enters `refresh`, sees that `inFlight` is set, and returns the same promise.
- Only one POST is sent. Both callers get the same token, or the same error.

`inFlight` is the promise returned by `.finally(...)`, so it is already reset to null by the time A or B resumes. A request that arrives after the refresh has settled will start a new one instead of reusing a stale result.

## Things to know before you change it

- **`inFlight` is shared across the whole module, not per store.** If two different stores (for example, two accounts) refresh at overlapping times, the second one receives the first one's token. Nothing is written to the second store, either.
- **Deduplication only works within one module instance.** Separate tabs, workers, or processes that share the same refresh token will each send their own POST. If the server rotates refresh tokens, the second POST can get a 401, and the `store.clear()` path would then log the user out.
- **The POST has no `Content-Type` header.** With a string body, fetch sends `text/plain;charset=UTF-8`. RFC 6749 specifies `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, so whether this works depends on how lenient your token server is.
- **If the response has no `expires_in`, `expiresAt` becomes `NaN`.** The check in `currentToken` then always fails, so every call triggers a refresh.

Wait until every service has loaded it, which includes any JWKS cache TTL. If you skip the wait, a service that hasn't loaded the new key will reject tokens signed with it.
3. **Switch signing to the new key.** New tokens get the new `kid`. Existing tokens still verify against the old key.
4. **Keep the old key until its tokens expire.** That means the longest lifetime of any token signed with it. If your refresh tokens are JWTs signed with the same key, that's the refresh-token lifetime, not the access-token lifetime.
5. **Remove the old key** from the verification set.

**Security warning:** this only applies to routine rotation. If you're rotating because the old key leaked, don't keep it around for verification. Anyone holding it can forge tokens until you remove it. Pull it right away, and accept that every token signed with it becomes invalid. Users stay logged in only if your refresh tokens are opaque and stored server-side, because those can still be exchanged for new access tokens signed with the new key.

## Normal path: `currentToken(store)`

`currentToken` (`auth.js:6`) reads `store.get('access')` and returns its value if more than `SKEW_MS` (30 seconds) of lifetime remains. If the token is missing, expired, or inside that 30-second window, it calls `refresh(store)`. The skew means a token is never handed out when it might expire while the request is in transit.

## Refresh: `refresh(store)`

1. If a refresh is already in flight, `refresh` returns the existing promise (`auth.js:13`). This is covered under concurrency below.
2. It reads `store.get('refresh')`. If no refresh token exists, it rejects with `no refresh token; re-auth required`.
3. It POSTs `{ grant_type: 'refresh_token', refresh_token }` to `/oauth/token` and stores the resulting promise in the module-level `inFlight`.
4. The response is handled in one of four ways:
   - **Success:** it stores the new access token with `expiresAt = now + expires_in * 1000`. If the server rotated the refresh token, it stores the new one too; otherwise the old one stays. It then resolves with the access token.
   - **401 from the token endpoint:** it calls `store.clear()` and rejects with `refresh rejected; re-auth required`. `clear()` wipes the whole store, not just the tokens. Any later call then fails at step 2 with `no refresh token`.
   - **Any other non-2xx status:** it rejects with `refresh failed: <status>` and leaves the store alone, so the next call tries the same refresh token again.
   - **Network error:** the `fetch` rejection propagates, and the store is also left alone.
5. `.finally` resets `inFlight = null` whether the refresh succeeded or failed (`auth.js:34`). On success the store is written before this runs, so a caller arriving afterwards finds the fresh token in `currentToken` and never reaches `refresh`.

## A 401 from an API call is not handled

The only 401 this file handles is one from `/oauth/token`. If an ordinary API request gets a 401, for example because the token was revoked on the server before its local `expiresAt`, nothing here retries or refreshes. `currentToken` will keep returning that cached token until it is within 30 seconds of expiry. A retry-on-401 would have to be written in the caller or added to this module.

## Two requests refreshing at once

Suppose request A calls `currentToken()`, finds the token expired, and calls `refresh()`. `inFlight` is null, so A starts the fetch and assigns the promise to `inFlight`. Request B then calls `currentToken()`. The store hasn't been updated yet, so B also calls `refresh()`, finds `inFlight` set, and gets the same promise. Both resolve with the same token, or both reject with the same error, including the 401 case.

The check at line 13 and the assignment at line 16 are not separated by an `await`, so they run in a single synchronous step. Two callers cannot both see `inFlight` as null.

If your app ever uses two stores, such as two accounts, and both refresh at the same moment, the second caller gets the first store's promise. That means it receives the other account's token, and its own store is never updated.

`auth.js` handles one thing: it gives callers a valid access token and refreshes it when it is close to expiring. Nothing in this file sends the API requests themselves.

## Normal flow

1. A caller asks for a token through `currentToken(store)` (`auth.js:6`). If the stored `access` token has more than 30 seconds left (`SKEW_MS`), it returns the token straight away. Otherwise it calls `refresh(store)`. The 30-second margin keeps a token from expiring while a request is on its way.
2. `refresh` reads the `refresh` token from the store. If there isn't one, it throws `no refresh token; re-auth required` and makes no network call (`auth.js:15`).
3. It POSTs to `/oauth/token` with `grant_type: 'refresh_token'` (`auth.js:16`).
4. On success it saves the new access token, with `expiresAt` set to now plus `expires_in` seconds. It replaces the stored refresh token only if the response includes a new one, so rotating and non-rotating servers both work. Then it returns the new access token (`auth.js:26-32`).
5. `.finally` sets `inFlight` back to `null` whether the refresh worked or failed, so the next refresh makes a fresh call (`auth.js:34`).

## What happens on a 401

There are two kinds of 401, and this file handles only one of them.

- **A 401 from `/oauth/token`.** The server has rejected the refresh token. The code calls `store.clear()`, which deletes both tokens, and throws `refresh rejected; re-auth required`. Every caller after that hits the "no refresh token" error at step 2 until the user logs in again.
- **A 401 from your actual API call.** Nothing in this file deals with it. If the server revokes an access token before its `expiresAt`, `currentToken` keeps returning it until it expires. To recover, the caller must catch the 401 and call `refresh(store)` directly, because `refresh` skips the expiry check.

Other failures leave the store alone. A 5xx response throws `refresh failed: <status>`. A network error rejects with whatever error `fetch` raises, unwrapped. In both cases the tokens stay in place, so the next call tries again.

## When two requests refresh at once

The module-level `inFlight` promise merges them into one call. Lines 13–16 run synchronously, with no `await` between checking `inFlight` and setting it, so two callers in the same JS context can't both start a refresh. The second caller gets the first caller's promise back. Both receive the same token, or the same rejection: if the refresh gets a 401, every waiting caller sees `refresh rejected`.

Before you change it, know that this merging has two limits:

- **It works only inside one module instance.** Separate tabs, workers, or processes each have their own `inFlight`. If your server rotates refresh tokens and detects reuse, two tabs refreshing at once can send the same refresh token twice. The server may then return 401 to the second one, and that tab will clear its store.
- **`inFlight` isn't tied to a store.** If you call `refresh(storeA)` and then `refresh(storeB)` before the first finishes, the second call gets storeA's token back, and storeB is never updated.

Despite the comment on line 1, the file doesn't attach headers or retry anything either. It only hands out tokens through `currentToken`, and the code that calls it does the rest.

## Normal path: `currentToken(store)` (lines 6–10)

1. It reads `access` from the store.
2. If the token exists and has more than `SKEW_MS` (30 s) left before `expiresAt`, it returns `t.value` straight away. The 30-second margin means a token that is about to expire is treated as already expired, so it can't run out while a request is on its way.
3. Otherwise it calls `refresh(store)` and returns the result.

## Refresh: `refresh(store)` (lines 12–38)

1. If a refresh is already running (`inFlight` is set), it returns that same promise and does nothing else.
2. It reads `refresh` from the store. If there is no refresh token, it throws `'no refresh token; re-auth required'`. This happens before `inFlight` is set, so the error belongs to this one call only.
3. It POSTs `grant_type: 'refresh_token'` to `/oauth/token` and stores the resulting promise in `inFlight`.
4. When the response arrives:

   - **Any other non-2xx response:** it throws `'refresh failed: ' + res.status` and leaves the store alone, so the next call tries again with the same refresh token.
   - **Success:** it stores the new access token with `expiresAt = now + expires_in * 1000`. If the server sent a new `refresh_token`, that replaces the old one; otherwise the old one is kept.
5. `.finally` sets `inFlight` back to `null` whether the refresh succeeded or failed.

## Two requests refreshing at once

JavaScript runs one thing at a time, and everything from the `if (inFlight)` check to the `inFlight = fetch(...)` assignment runs without pausing. So when the first request starts a refresh, `inFlight` is already set before any other code can run. The second request finds it and gets the same promise back. Only one POST goes out. Both callers get the same token, or the same error if the refresh fails, and on a 401 `store.clear()` runs only once. Any call that arrives after `.finally` has run starts a new refresh. By then a successful refresh has already stored the new token, so `currentToken` usually finds it fresh and doesn't need to refresh at all.

## Things to keep in mind before changing it

- **`inFlight` is shared across the whole module, not kept per store.** If two different `store` objects (say, two accounts) refresh at the same time, the second one gets the first one's promise. It receives the first account's token, and its own store is never updated.
- **`refresh` is exported.** Code outside this file can call it directly, and probably does for API 401s. Look at those callers before you change how `refresh` behaves.

**Normal path.** `currentToken(store)` reads `access` from the store. If the token exists and has more than 30 seconds (`SKEW_MS`) left before `expiresAt`, it returns the cached value without any network call. Otherwise it calls `refresh(store)`. 1. If an `inFlight` promise already exists, it returns that promise (see the concurrency section).
2. It reads `refresh` from the store. If there isn't one, it rejects with `no refresh token; re-auth required` and makes no network call.
3. It POSTs `{ grant_type: 'refresh_token', refresh_token }` to `/oauth/token` and stores the whole promise chain in `inFlight`.

The working directory is empty, so I couldn't check your setup. This is the standard procedure: for a while, the verifiers accept both the old and new keys, while only the new key signs.

1. **Add a `kid` (key ID) header to tokens.** Each verifier should pick the key by `kid` from a key set, such as a JWKS endpoint or a config map. If your current tokens have no `kid`, have verifiers treat a missing `kid` as the old key.
2. **Add the new key to every verifier's key set and deploy that first.** Don't sign with it yet. If a service that hasn't picked up the new key receives a new token, it will reject it.
3. **Switch signing to the new key.** Only do this after every verifier has the new key, including any JWKS caches past their cache lifetime.
4. **Wait out the longest-lived old token.** That is the access token TTL. If your refresh tokens are also JWTs signed with this key, it's the refresh token lifetime instead, which is usually much longer.
5. **Remove the old key from the verification set.**

Users stay logged in because their existing tokens keep verifying until they expire. Any token issued or refreshed after step 3 uses the new key.

This doesn't apply if you're rotating because the key leaked. Then the old key has to be removed right away, which invalidates every token it signed. Users who have opaque, server-stored refresh tokens can still silently get new access tokens. Everyone else has to log in again.

There's one thing to know first: **this file has no retry-on-401 for your API requests.** The only 401 it handles comes from the refresh endpoint itself. If an API call returns 401 because the server revoked a token that hasn't expired yet, that has to be handled by whatever calls `currentToken()`, or it isn't handled at all.

## Normal flow

1. A request calls `currentToken(store)` (`auth.js:6`).
2. If there is an access token and it expires more than `SKEW_MS` (30 seconds) from now, the cached value is returned. Otherwise it calls `refresh(store)`. The 30-second margin keeps a token from expiring while a request is in transit.
3. `refresh` reads the refresh token. If there isn't one, it throws `no refresh token; re-auth required` without making a network call (`auth.js:15`).
4. It POSTs `grant_type: refresh_token` to `/oauth/token`.
5. On success it stores the new access token with `expiresAt = now + expires_in * 1000`. If the response includes a new `refresh_token` (rotation), it replaces the stored one; otherwise the old one is kept. Then it returns the new access token.

## Failure paths

- **The refresh endpoint returns 401** (`auth.js:21`): it calls `store.clear()`, which wipes both tokens, and throws `refresh rejected; re-auth required`. After that, every call fails at step 3 until the user logs in again.
- **Other non-OK status, such as a 500:** it throws `refresh failed: <status>` and leaves the store alone. The next `currentToken()` call tries the refresh again. Nothing limits how often that happens.
- **Network error:** `fetch` rejects, the `.then` is skipped, and the error goes to the caller. The store is left alone, as with a 500.

In every case, `.finally` resets `inFlight` to `null`, so a failed refresh never blocks the next attempt.

## Two requests refreshing at once

`inFlight` is a module-level variable holding the promise of the current refresh.

- Request A finds the token expired, calls `refresh()`, sees `inFlight` is null, and starts the fetch. `inFlight` is set in the same synchronous step as the check, so no second caller can get in between.
- Request B arrives while that fetch is pending. It hits `if (inFlight) return inFlight` and gets the same promise. Only one POST goes out.
- Both receive the same result: the same new token on success, or the same error on failure. On a 401, both get the rejection, and the store is cleared once.
- `.finally` clears `inFlight` before A and B resume, so the next expiry starts a new refresh.

There are two limits to that deduplication you should know before changing it:

- **`inFlight` is shared by every `store`, not kept per store.** If one process uses more than one store (for example, several users or accounts), store 2 calling `refresh` while store 1's refresh is pending gets store 1's access token, and store 2's own tokens are never updated.
- **It only works within one module instance.** Separate browser tabs, workers or processes each have their own `inFlight`, so they can send the same refresh token at the same time. If the server rotates refresh tokens and detects reuse, the losing request gets a 401, which clears that instance's store and logs the user out.

The usual method is to give each key an ID and run old and new keys side by side for a while. Do these steps in order:

1. Generate the new key and give it a new key ID (`kid`).
2. Add the new key to the set of keys your services accept, and keep the old key in that set. Deploy this to every service that checks tokens before anything starts signing with the new key. If you use RS256 or ES256, publishing both public keys at your JWKS endpoint does this.
3. Switch signing to the new key, and put its `kid` in each token's header so services know which key to check against. Tokens issued so far have no `kid`, so services should check those against the old key.
4. Keep the old key accepted until the longest-lived token it signed has expired. Usually that is your access-token lifetime. If your refresh tokens are JWTs signed with the same key, wait out the refresh-token lifetime instead.
5. Remove the old key from the accepted set.

Users stay logged in because a token is never checked against a set that lacks the key that signed it.

**If you are rotating because the old key leaked, skip the overlap.** Stop accepting the old key immediately. Anyone holding it can forge valid tokens for as long as it is accepted. Every user will be logged out, and that is unavoidable here.

`auth.js` has two exported functions. `currentToken` decides whether a refresh is needed, and `refresh` does the refresh and makes concurrent callers share one network call.

## Normal flow

1. `currentToken(store)` reads `store.get('access')` (`auth.js:7`). If a token exists and has more than `SKEW_MS` (30 seconds) left before `expiresAt`, it returns `t.value` and does nothing else. A token with less than 30 seconds left counts as expired, so it gets refreshed early instead of expiring while a request is in flight.
2. Otherwise it calls `refresh(store)` (`auth.js:9`).
3. `refresh` first checks `inFlight`. If a refresh is already running, it returns that same promise (`auth.js:13`).
4. If not, it reads the refresh token. If there isn't one, it throws `no refresh token; re-auth required` and leaves the store alone (`auth.js:15`).
5. It POSTs `grant_type: 'refresh_token'` to `/oauth/token` and stores the resulting promise in `inFlight` (`auth.js:16`).
6. On success, it stores the new access token with `expiresAt = Date.now() + expires_in * 1000`. If the server sent back a new `refresh_token`, it replaces the old one; if not, the old one stays (`auth.js:27-31`). It then resolves with the new access token.
7. `.finally` sets `inFlight` back to `null` whether the refresh succeeded or failed (`auth.js:34-36`).

## What happens on a 401

The only 401 this file handles is a 401 from the token endpoint itself, meaning the refresh token was rejected. In that case it calls `store.clear()`, which wipes the whole store (both tokens and anything else in it), and throws `refresh rejected; re-auth required` (`auth.js:21-23`). Any other non-OK status throws `refresh failed: <status>` and leaves the tokens in place, so the next `currentToken` call will try to refresh again.

A 401 from one of your API requests is not handled anywhere in this file. There is no retry-on-401 logic. If your callers handle that case, they do it themselves, probably by calling the exported `refresh(store)` directly. That forces a refresh even when the stored token still looks valid.

## Two requests refreshing at once

The deduplication works because JavaScript runs on one thread. Request A calls `refresh`, and everything up to the assignment of `inFlight` runs synchronously, because `fetch(...).then(...).finally(...)` returns a promise immediately. So by the time request B gets to run, `inFlight` is already set. B returns the same promise and gets the same token, or the same error, as A. Only one POST goes out.

`inFlight` points at the promise returned by `.finally()`, so it is already `null` when any waiting caller resumes. A request that arrives after the refresh finishes finds the fresh token in the store and never calls `refresh`.

One thing to watch when you change it: `inFlight` is a module-level variable, not tied to a particular store (`auth.js:4`). If your app uses more than one store, for example two accounts, and they refresh at the same moment, the second caller gets the first store's promise. That means it receives the first account's access token, and its own store is never refreshed. The deduplication is only correct if there is exactly one store per process.

**Normal path**

1. Every request calls `currentToken(store)` (line 6). If the stored access token has more than 30 seconds left (`SKEW_MS`), the function returns it without touching the network.
2. If the token is missing, expired, or within 30 seconds of expiry, it calls `refresh(store)` instead.
3. `refresh` reads the refresh token. If there isn't one, it rejects with `no refresh token; re-auth required` and makes no request.
4. It POSTs `{ grant_type: 'refresh_token', refresh_token }` to `/oauth/token` and saves that promise in the module-level `inFlight` variable.
5. On success, it stores the new access token with `expiresAt = now + expires_in * 1000`. If the response includes a new refresh token (rotation), that replaces the old one; otherwise the old one is kept. The promise resolves to the new access token.
6. `.finally` sets `inFlight` back to `null` on both success and failure, so the next refresh starts a new request.

The only 401 this file handles comes from the token endpoint. On that 401, the code calls `store.clear()`, which wipes both tokens, and rejects with `refresh rejected; re-auth required`. After that, every call fails at step 3 with `no refresh token` until the user logs in again.

- RFC 6749 says a server should reject an expired or revoked refresh token with 400 `invalid_grant`. A 401 means client authentication failed. If your server follows the spec, a dead refresh token lands in the `refresh failed: 400` branch instead. The store never gets cleared, and every request retries the dead token. Check which status your server actually sends.

**Two requests refreshing at once**

`refresh` assigns `inFlight` before any `await`, so the first caller sets it in the same synchronous step. A second caller that arrives before the promise settles hits line 13 and gets that same promise back. Only one POST goes out, and both callers get the same token or the same error. The new token is written to the store before `.finally` runs, so later callers take the cached path in step 1.

The deduplication has two limits:

- `inFlight` is shared by the whole module, not kept per `store`. Suppose two different stores refresh at the same time, such as two users in one server process. The second caller gets the first store's token, and its own store is never updated.

The working directory is empty, so I couldn't see your code. This is the standard approach.

Run a short period where both keys are accepted, using the `kid` (key ID) header to tell them apart:

1. **Add the new key to verification only.** Generate it, give it a new `kid`, and publish it next to the old key in your JWKS or verifier configuration. Keep signing with the old key. Wait until every verifier has picked up the new key set, which means at least as long as the JWKS cache TTL.
2. **Switch signing to the new key.** New tokens carry the new `kid`. Existing tokens still verify against the old key, so nobody is logged out.
3. **Keep the old key until the longest-lived token signed with it has expired.** For access tokens that is their TTL. If your refresh tokens are JWTs signed with the same key, the wait is the refresh token lifetime, which can be weeks. Opaque refresh tokens stored in a database aren't affected by the signing key, so the overlap only has to cover the access token TTL.
4. **Remove the old key** from the verification set.

If your current tokens have no `kid`, have verifiers treat a missing `kid` as the old key until those tokens expire.

Two security points:

- **If the key was compromised, skip the overlap.** Remove the old key immediately. The only way to avoid logging everyone out is opaque refresh tokens: clients get new access tokens from them, signed with the new key.
- **Look up `kid` only in your own allowlist of keys, and pin the algorithm on the server side.** Never use `kid` to build a file path, URL, or database query, and never trust the token's `alg` header. Both are well-known ways to forge tokens.

**Normal path**

1. `currentToken(store)` reads `store.get('access')`. If a token exists and has more than `SKEW_MS` (30 seconds) left before `expiresAt`, it returns that token with no network call (`auth.js:8`).
2. Otherwise it calls `refresh(store)`. If a refresh is already running, `refresh` returns that same promise (`auth.js:13`; see the concurrency section below).
3. It reads `store.get('refresh')`. If there is no refresh token, it rejects with `no refresh token; re-auth required`. This happens before `inFlight` is set, so nothing is shared and nothing needs cleaning up.
4. It POSTs `{ grant_type: 'refresh_token', refresh_token }` to `/oauth/token` as a JSON string. No `Content-Type` header is set, so fetch sends the body as `text/plain;charset=UTF-8`.
5. On a 2xx response it stores the new access token with `expiresAt = Date.now() + expires_in * 1000`, timed from when the response arrives. It replaces the refresh token only if the server sent a new one. Then it resolves with the access token.
6. `.finally` resets `inFlight` to `null`, whether the refresh succeeded or failed.

**On a 401**

The only 401 this file handles is one from `/oauth/token` itself, which means the refresh token was rejected. In that case it calls `store.clear()`, which wipes the access token, the refresh token and everything else in the store, and then rejects with `refresh rejected; re-auth required`. Any other non-2xx status rejects with `refresh failed: <status>` and leaves the store alone, so the next call tries the refresh again.

A 401 from an ordinary API call is not handled here at all. If a token is revoked before its `expiresAt`, `currentToken` keeps returning it until it is within 30 seconds of expiry. Retrying after a 401 would have to happen in the caller, by calling the exported `refresh(store)` directly.

**Two requests refreshing at once**

Request A calls `currentToken()`, finds the token expired, and calls `refresh()`. `refresh()` checks `inFlight` and assigns the fetch promise to it synchronously, before anything yields, so no other request can get in between the check and the assignment. Request B then finds the same expired token, because the store hasn't been updated yet, and calls `refresh()`. It sees `inFlight` and gets the same promise back. Both requests end up with the same token, or the same error.

Only one refresh token gets used, and that matters if the server rotates refresh tokens. A second refresh with the already-used token would get a 401, take the path above, and clear the store, which logs the user out.

This deduplication has two limits:

- `inFlight` is a module-level variable, not tracked per store. If two different stores refresh at the same moment, the second caller receives the first store's access token, and its own store is never updated.
- It only deduplicates within one module instance. If the store is backed by storage shared across tabs, workers or processes, each of those refreshes on its own. With rotating refresh tokens, whichever one loses the race hits the 401 path and clears the shared store for all of them.

```bash
find / -type f -size +100M -mtime -7 2>/dev/null
```

What each part does:

- `/` is the starting directory. `find` searches it recursively, so replace it with `.` or `~` to narrow the search.
- `-type f` matches only regular files, not directories or symlinks.
- `-size +100M` matches files larger than 100 MiB. The `+` means "more than." `M` counts in mebibytes (1024², or 1,048,576 bytes), and `find` rounds sizes up to whole units, so a file just over 100 MiB counts as 101 and matches.
- `-mtime -7` matches files whose contents were modified less than 7 days ago, counted in 24-hour periods back from now rather than from calendar days. The `-` means "less than."
- `2>/dev/null` throws away error output, mostly the "Permission denied" messages you get when scanning `/` as a normal user.

To show sizes and sort by largest first, use this version:

```bash
find / -type f -size +100M -mtime -7 -exec du -h {} + 2>/dev/null | sort -rh
```

Here `-exec du -h {} +` passes the matching files to `du` in batches, and `sort -rh` sorts the human-readable sizes in descending order.

Run a period where both keys are accepted. Sign new tokens with the new key, keep accepting the old key, and remove it only after every token it signed has expired.

1. **Make sure verifiers can hold more than one key.** Put a `kid` (key ID) in each token's header and have verifiers look up the key by `kid`, from a JWKS endpoint or a key map in configuration. If you can't add `kid` yet, verifiers can try the new key first and fall back to the old one.
2. **Add the new key to verification only.** Deploy it to every service that verifies tokens, and keep signing with the old key. Wait until all verifiers have the new key, including any that cache the JWKS.
3. **Switch signing to the new key.** New logins and token refreshes now get tokens signed with it. Old tokens still verify.
4. **Wait out the longest token lifetime.** This is the access-token TTL. If your refresh tokens are JWTs signed with the same key, it's their TTL instead, which may be weeks.
5. **Remove the old key** from the verification set.

Refresh tokens decide how long step 4 takes:

- **Opaque refresh tokens (database-backed):** these aren't affected by the key change. Users get new-key access tokens on their next refresh, so the wait is only the access-token TTL.
- **Long-lived JWT refresh tokens:** keep the old key for their full lifetime. Or re-issue them with the new key on each refresh, and accept that users inactive for the whole window get logged out.

**Security warning:** if you're rotating because the old key leaked, don't use an overlap period. Anyone with the leaked key can create valid tokens until you stop accepting it. Remove the old key immediately and accept the forced re-login. You can soften that only if refresh tokens are checked against a database rather than by the signing key.

`auth.js` refreshes tokens before they expire. It never reacts to a 401 from your API. The only 401 it handles is one from the token endpoint itself.

## Normal path: `currentToken(store)`

`auth.js:7-9` reads the `access` entry. If the entry exists and has more than `SKEW_MS` (30 seconds) of life left, its value is returned with no network call. If it is missing, expired, or inside that 30-second window, the function calls `refresh(store)` and returns that result.

## Refresh: `refresh(store)`

1. **Join a refresh already running** (`auth.js:13`): if `inFlight` is set, the caller gets the existing promise and no second request goes out.
2. **Check for a refresh token** (`auth.js:14-15`): if there is none, the call rejects with `no refresh token; re-auth required`. Because `refresh` is `async`, this is a rejected promise, not a synchronous throw.
3. **Call the token endpoint** (`auth.js:16-19`): it POSTs `grant_type=refresh_token` as JSON to `/oauth/token` and stores the promise in `inFlight` before anything awaits.
4. **Handle the response** (`auth.js:20-32`):
   - **401:** `store.clear()` wipes the whole store, not just the tokens, and the call rejects with `refresh rejected; re-auth required`.
   - **Any other non-2xx:** the call rejects with `refresh failed: <status>`. The store is left alone, so the next call retries with the same refresh token.
   - **Success:** the new access token is saved with `expiresAt = now + expires_in * 1000`. The refresh token is replaced only if the server sent a new one (rotation), and the access token is returned.
5. **Cleanup** (`auth.js:34-36`): `finally` clears `inFlight` whether the call succeeded or failed. Callers' `await`s settle after that step, so by the time any caller sees the result, the store is updated and the next refresh can start.

## Two requests refreshing at once

Request A calls `currentToken()`, finds the token expired, and enters `refresh()`. No `await` runs between the `inFlight` check on line 13 and the assignment on line 16, so nothing can interleave there. Request B then finds the same expired token, calls `refresh()`, sees `inFlight`, and gets A's promise. One HTTP request goes out, and both callers get the same token or the same error.

That deduplication has two limits:

- **`inFlight` is shared by every store in the module, but `store` is a parameter.** If two different stores refresh at the same time (for example, two users on a server), the second caller gets the first store's token, and its own store is never updated. That is a real bug if you ever pass more than one store.
- **It works only within one JavaScript context.** Separate tabs, workers, or processes each have their own `inFlight`. With refresh-token rotation (line 31), two of them can send the same refresh token. Servers that detect reuse may reject one of them or revoke the whole token family.

## What "on a 401" actually covers

- **401s from your API are not handled.** If the server revokes an access token early, the caller gets the 401, and nothing here retries. To add that, you would call the exported `refresh()` and retry the request. Note that `refresh()` doesn't check whether the token is already fresh, so several requests failing with 401 after a refresh finishes would each start another refresh.
- **A dead refresh token may not return 401.** Under the OAuth spec (RFC 6749 §5.2), an invalid or revoked refresh token gets `400 invalid_grant`, and 401 is for failed client authentication. If your server follows the spec, a revoked session takes the `refresh failed: 400` path. The store isn't cleared, and every later call retries the same dead token. Check what your token endpoint really returns.

## One edge case in the expiry math

If a response leaves out `expires_in`, `expiresAt` becomes `NaN`, and the check on line 8 is always false. Every `currentToken()` call then triggers a refresh. Tokens that live 30 seconds or less behave the same way.

Everything is in `auth.js`, and its 40 lines cover the whole flow.

**Normal path**

1. `currentToken(store)` reads `access` from the store. If the token exists and has more than 30 seconds left (`SKEW_MS`), it returns the cached value with no network call (auth.js:7-8).
2. Otherwise it calls `refresh(store)`. If there is no refresh token stored, the call fails with `no refresh token; re-auth required` (auth.js:15).
3. `refresh` POSTs the refresh token to `/oauth/token`. On success, it stores the new access token with `expiresAt = now + expires_in`. It replaces the refresh token only if the server sent a new one. Then it returns the access token (auth.js:26-32).
4. `.finally` sets `inFlight` back to `null` whether the call succeeded or failed, so the next expiry starts a fresh refresh.

**On a 401**

The only 401 this file handles is one from the token endpoint itself. In that case it calls `store.clear()`, which wipes both tokens and anything else in the store, and fails with `refresh rejected; re-auth required`. Any other non-OK status, or a network error, also fails but leaves the store alone, so the next request tries to refresh again.

Two consequences:

- **401s from normal API calls are not handled.** If the API rejects an access token that still looks valid locally (because it was revoked, or the clocks disagree), `currentToken` keeps returning it until it gets close to expiry. To force a refresh, the caller has to call the exported `refresh(store)` directly, which skips the expiry check.
- **Your server may never send that 401.** Standard OAuth servers (RFC 6749 §5.2) answer an expired or revoked refresh token with 400 `invalid_grant`, not 401. If yours does that, the clear-and-re-auth branch never runs. Instead, every request fails with `refresh failed: 400`, and the dead refresh token stays in the store. **Two refreshes at once**

Any caller that arrives before the refresh finishes gets the same promise back at line 13. Only one POST goes out, and every waiting caller gets the same token or the same error. By the time those callers resume, `finally` has already reset `inFlight` and the store holds the new token, so later callers just use the cached token.

2. **Publish the new key before you sign with it.** Add it to the verification key set (your JWKS endpoint, or the config every service reads). It reads `access` from the store. If that token exists and has more than 30 seconds (`SKEW_MS`) left, it returns it. Otherwise it calls `refresh(store)`. The 30-second margin refreshes tokens early so they don't expire while a request is still in transit.

**Refreshing** (`refresh`, `auth.js:12`)

No, raising the pool size would only delay the problem. You're most likely leaking connections. In `db.js:11-16`, `withClient` calls `client.release()` only when `fn` succeeds. If `fn` throws, that client is never returned to the pool.

The log fits that pattern. `idle` stays at 0 for the whole window and `waiting` keeps climbing from 7 to 28. If the pool were simply too small for the load, clients would sometimes go idle and the queue would rise and fall. A pool of 40 would fill up the same way, just later.

I wouldn't add a new cache layer. The CDN already in front of the app can do the caching. Its hit rate is 0% because `middleware/security.js:8` sends `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` on every response, `/p` included, and the CDN does whatever origin headers say (`CDN.md`).

**How to build it:** keep that middleware as the default and have the product route opt out on purpose. In `routes/products.js`, successful renders would set something like `Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60` and remove `Pragma`. The agreement with platform engineering says cache policy goes in response headers, so this is where it belongs.

**Security:** don't loosen the middleware for the whole app. `/account` has to stay `no-store`, because the 2024 audit finding was exactly that problem. Opting `/p` in is only safe while those pages stay anonymous. If session middleware, a `Set-Cookie`, or anything user-specific ever reaches `/p` responses, the CDN could serve one user's page to everyone.

**The decision that sets the TTL is stock.** The page shows `stockFor`, and inventory probably changes with orders, not just with the few admin edits a day. How out of date can the displayed stock be?

- If a few minutes is fine, cache the whole page.
- If not, cache the page and fetch stock separately with a short TTL or no caching.

Exact TTLs and purging the CDN when someone edits a product are details for later.

Have the browser poll `/api/metrics` on a timer. The platform rules out the push options:

- **WebSockets:** `PLATFORM.md` says the edge returns 501 on any upgrade.
- **Server-sent events or long-polling:** a function is killed at 10 seconds and frozen afterward, so it can't hold a stream open or watch for changes.
- **Faster polling:** the data only changes when the rollup job runs once a minute, so polling more often wouldn't show anything newer.

The change belongs entirely in `public/dashboard.js`:

1. After each fetch, schedule the next one for `computed_at` plus 60 seconds plus a few seconds of buffer, rather than a fixed `setInterval`. The buffer keeps the poll from landing while the job is truncating and rewriting the table.
2. Skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed. Also ignore any response with no rows, which can happen if a request catches the table mid-rewrite.
3. Pause polling when the tab is hidden, using `visibilitychange`, and fetch immediately when it becomes visible again.

`api/metrics.js` doesn't need to change. At 4KB and 30ms per request, one call a minute per open tab costs almost nothing.

The one decision for you is whether to keep the Refresh button. It can never show anything newer than the last poll, so I'd remove it and let the `stamp` timestamp show how fresh the data is. Retrying with backoff on failed fetches and ETag/304 responses are details for the next level down.

Upload directly from the phone to S3 with a signed PUT URL, so the photo bytes never pass through nginx or Express. You can't route them through the app: the global `client_max_body_size 1m` in `nginx.conf` can't be raised (the payments team declined that, including per-location overrides), and a phone photo is several MB. The rest is already in place. `storage.signedUrl` accepts `method: 'PUT'`, the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from market.example.com, and `listings.photo_keys` exists but has never been written to.

The flow takes three requests:

1. The client calls `POST /listings/:id/photos`. The server checks that the seller owns the listing, generates the key itself (`listings/<id>/photos/<uuid>.jpg`), and returns a signed PUT URL.
2. The client PUTs the file straight to S3.
3. The client sends the key to a confirm endpoint. The server checks that the key has this listing's prefix and that the object exists (`HeadObject`), then calls `db.addPhotoKey`.

To display photos, do what the invoice route does: sign a GET URL for each key in `photo_keys`.

Two security points:

- **Check the key prefix in step 3.** Invoices are in the same bucket. Without the check, a seller could submit another listing's `invoice_key` as a "photo," and the read path would give them a signed link to that invoice.
- **Strip location data.** Phone photos usually have GPS coordinates in their EXIF metadata, often the seller's home. Remove it before the photos are public.

The main open decision is where to resize the photos and strip EXIF:

- **In the browser:** re-encode on a canvas to about 2000px JPEG before uploading. This needs no new infrastructure and keeps uploads small, but a client that skips the step uploads the original.
- **On the server:** a Lambda triggered by the S3 upload. This guarantees it happens, but adds a processing pipeline and a "processing" state for photos.

Which matters more to you: guaranteeing the stripping happens, or not adding infrastructure? The next level of detail is a size cap and thumbnails. A plain signed PUT doesn't limit file size, so you'd need either a signed `ContentLength` or a presigned POST with `content-length-range`.

Yes. Assuming this is Postgres (the schema's `BIGSERIAL` and `TIMESTAMPTZ` suggest so), a plain `DROP TABLE users;` will fail, and the obvious workaround does damage you won't see.

1. **The plain drop errors out.** Both `sessions.user_id` and `invoices.user_id` have foreign keys to `users(id)`, so you'll get `ERROR: cannot drop table users because other objects depend on it`.
2. **`DROP TABLE users CASCADE` doesn't delete sessions or invoices.** It only removes their foreign key constraints. The `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `sessions` applies when rows are deleted, not when the table is dropped. If you then recreate `users`, both tables keep their rows but lose the constraint, so nothing checks `user_id` anymore. You also can't rerun all of `schema.sql`, because `CREATE TABLE sessions` and `CREATE TABLE invoices` will fail on tables that already exist.
3. **Old rows will point at the new users.** `fixtures/users.json` has no ids, so Ada and Grace get ids 1 and 2 from the new sequence. Any existing invoice or session with `user_id` 1 or 2 will then belong to them, and the rest will point at users that don't exist. Invoices were left without `ON DELETE CASCADE`, which suggests someone meant to protect them.

If this is a dev database and you want a clean reset, use this instead of the drop:

```sql
TRUNCATE users, sessions, invoices RESTART IDENTITY;
```

This permanently deletes every row in all three tables, including the invoices. If any of that data matters, back it up first with `pg_dump -t users -t sessions -t invoices`.

The directory is empty, so this is the general method rather than one tailored to your code. The idea is to run both keys side by side for a while: verifiers accept the old key and the new one, signing moves to the new key, and the old key is removed only after every token it signed has expired.

1. **Make verification select the key by `kid`.** Every token should carry a `kid` header, and verifiers should look that ID up in a set of accepted keys (a JWKS endpoint, or a key map/list for HS256 secrets) instead of using one hard-coded key. If you don't have this yet, deploy it first, with the current key as the only entry.
2. **Publish the new key to verifiers before anything signs with it.** Add it to the accepted set and wait until every service has it, including any JWKS cache TTL.
3. **Switch signing to the new key.** New tokens get the new `kid`, and old tokens still verify against the old key.
4. **Keep the old key in the verify set for the lifetime of the longest-lived token it signed.** For access tokens alone that is usually minutes to hours. If your refresh tokens are JWTs signed with the same key, the window is the refresh token lifetime, unless your refresh handler re-issues tokens with the new key.
5. **Remove the old key** once that window has passed.

**Security caveat:** this only applies to scheduled rotation. If the old key may be compromised, remove it right away. Anyone holding it can forge tokens for as long as verifiers accept it, so logging everyone out is the price of closing that hole.

`auth.js` refreshes lazily. Nothing runs on a timer; a refresh happens only when a request needs a token and the stored one won't do.

## Normal path

1. Every request calls `currentToken(store)` (`auth.js:6`). If the stored access token has more than 30 seconds (`SKEW_MS`) left, that token is returned and nothing else happens. If the token is missing, expired, or within 30 seconds of expiring, it calls `refresh(store)`.
2. `refresh` (`auth.js:12`) reads the refresh token. If there isn't one, it rejects with `no refresh token; re-auth required`.
3. It POSTs `grant_type: refresh_token` to `/oauth/token`.
4. On success it saves the new access token with `expiresAt = Date.now() + expires_in * 1000`. It saves a new refresh token only if the server sent one; otherwise the old one stays. It then resolves with the access token.

## What happens on a 401

The only 401 this file handles is one from the token endpoint, which means the server rejected the refresh token. In that case it calls `store.clear()`, which wipes the whole store, refresh token included, and rejects with `refresh rejected; re-auth required`. Every later call then fails with `no refresh token; re-auth required` until the user signs in again.

Any other failure leaves the store untouched, so the next request retries with the same refresh token. That covers a non-2xx status (which rejects with `refresh failed: <status>`), a network error, and a response body that isn't valid JSON.

A 401 from your API is not handled in this file, and nothing here retries a failed request. If code elsewhere calls the exported `refresh` when it gets an API 401, be aware that `refresh` never checks whether the token is already fresh. A 401 that arrives after another refresh has finished will start a second refresh.

## Two requests refreshing at once

Request A finds the token expired and calls `refresh`. `inFlight` is null, so A starts the fetch and stores the promise in `inFlight`. Request B arrives before the response comes back. It also finds the token expired, because the store hasn't been updated yet. It calls `refresh`, sees `inFlight`, and gets the same promise back. Only one network call is made, and both requests get the same token or the same error. On a 401, both are rejected.

Two callers can't both pass the check on line 13, because there's no `await` between that check and the assignment on line 16.

Once the fetch settles, `finally` sets `inFlight` back to null. The store is written before that point, so a request that arrives afterwards gets the new token straight from `currentToken` and doesn't trigger another refresh.

One catch: `inFlight` is shared by the whole module, not kept per store. Suppose two stores exist in the same process, for example for two accounts, and both refresh at the same time. The second caller receives the first store's access token, and its own store is never updated.
